clue.text: Making shorter flight around British border — rural England initially

indicators.note: around says the word for flight is wrapped about the other letters

parts.note: aviation is the business of flying, flight

indicators.note: initially says take the opening letter of each of the three words before it

explanation.surface: A rural walk or flight path skirting the English border, described in a shortened form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' puts B plus BRE (the first letters of 'border rural England') inside AVIATION.
explanation.definitionFit: An abbreviation is the act of shortening a word or phrase, so the process noun matches 'making shorter'.

clue.text: Lament wrong grid (editor's first)

indicators.note: wrong signals that the letters of grid are set out incorrectly, rearranged
first here asks for the opening letter of editor's

explanation.surface: A crossword editor bemoaning a misprinted grid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' rearranges GRID to DIRG; 'first' takes E from 'editor's'.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirge is a mournful song or lament, typically sung at a funeral.

clue.text: Tip from forum I post in error

indicators.note: the tip of a word can be its end; here the final letter of forum

parts.note: a stake is a post driven into the ground

explanation.surface: Someone writing on an internet forum admits posting something by accident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' could be either end; only the last letter, M, fits. 'Post' looks like a verb about forums but is a wooden stake.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: an error is a slip or blunder made in doing something.

clue.text: Sailors, a part-time force, in decline

parts.note: ABs are able seamen, ordinary sailors
the TA, the Territorial Army, is Britain's reserve force of part-time soldiers

explanation.surface: Naval and reserve forces are said to be shrinking.
explanation.walkthrough: The TA (Territorial Army) is the British Army's volunteer reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: To decline an offer or vote is to refrain from it, a verb synonym.

clue.text: One going downhill fast or soaring?

definitions.meaning: someone racing down a snowy slope on skis
read whimsically as a comparative, more sky-high; also a cricket term for a ball hit high into the air

explanation.surface: Is the person flying down the slope racing or airborne?
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a pun: the word read as sky plus -er, something higher in the sky; in cricket the same word is a mistimed shot that soars upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on skis descending a slope at speed; and, punningly, a thing more lofty, sky-high.

clue.text: Blunder that gets one screaming?

definitions.meaning: someone who wails or yells loudly

explanation.surface: A mistake so bad it sets someone yelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that gets' is only linking: the second reading is a person or animal that yells.
explanation.definitionFit: Colloquially a glaring gaffe; literally, a creature that yells or wails, like a monkey of that name.

clue.text: Spies a place to go

parts.note: the gents is a men's public toilet in Britain, a euphemistic place to go

explanation.surface: Spies are given a location to head for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a place to go' reads as a destination, but 'go' is British slang for using the toilet; the gents is the men's lavatory.
explanation.definitionFit: Secret agents working for an intelligence service are spies.

clue.text: Peter out, going round nine or eleven Southern states

indicators.note: going round says the verb for fading is wrapped about the numerals

parts.note: to peter out is to fade away, die
IX is Roman nine; the setter notes that inserted after D, the result equally reads as XI, Roman eleven, after the first I

explanation.surface: A trend fading out across the southern US states.
explanation.walkthrough: The neat trick: putting IX (nine) in DIE after the D gives the same letters as putting XI (eleven) after DI, so either number works.
explanation.definitionFit: Dixie is the nickname for the southern states of the USA, the old Confederacy.

clue.text: Newspaper cutting English and German articles in two?

indicators.note: cutting says the paper's name splits the two articles apart

parts.note: A is the English indefinite article, DER the German definite article
the Sun is a British tabloid newspaper

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor slicing up pieces written in English and German.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British daily tabloid. 'cutting' looks like a press cutting but means going into A...DER.
explanation.definitionFit: Torn apart into pieces, split in two, as in 'rent asunder'.

clue.text: New poet is a source of false contentment?

indicators.note: new signals a fresh arrangement of the letters that follow

explanation.surface: A newly arrived poet is seen as a provider of comfortable illusions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges POET IS A.
explanation.definitionFit: Narcotic drugs from the poppy induce a dreamy, false sense of well-being.

clue.text: Came to pass in Andes or Alps, when returning

indicators.note: when returning says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Something happened in the mountains on the way back.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters ESORA span 'Andes or Alps'; 'when returning' turns them round.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: something that arose happened, occurred or came about.

clue.text: Hints people changed around following editor's bungle?

indicators.note: around says the rearranged letters surround the abbreviation
changed signals that the letters of hints people are reordered

parts.note: f is the abbreviation for following, as in page references

explanation.surface: People altered suggestions after an editor made a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed' rearranges HINTS PEOPLE, and 'around' wraps those letters about F.
explanation.definitionFit: A careless written error, the kind an editor might make with a stroke of the nib.

clue.text: Knocking on a bit? More than that!

definitions.text: Knocking on a bit? More than that!

parts.words: Knocking on a bit? More than that!
parts.note: knocking on a bit is British slang for getting old; someone close to dying is further along, and knocking suggests rapping at a portal

explanation.surface: Someone ageing, perhaps worse off than merely old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocking on a bit' is British for elderly; the answer goes further, near dying, with a pun on knocking at a door.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for being on the brink of dying, worse than simply growing old.

clue.text: Goes too far when toasting poet

definitions.meaning: bread overdone under the grill chars and blackens
Scotland's national poet, author of Auld Lang Syne

explanation.surface: A speaker overdoes it when raising a glass to a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'toasting' looks like raising a glass, as at a Scottish poet's supper, but means grilling bread.
explanation.definitionFit: Overdone toast chars; and Robert of that surname is Scotland's national bard.

clue.text: Transport around English village initially providing lift

indicators.note: around says the word for delight wraps about the other letters

parts.note: to transport someone with joy is to elate them

indicators.note: initially takes the opening letter of village

explanation.surface: Transport laid on around an English village gives people a lift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transport' looks like vehicles but means delight. 'around' puts E and V inside ELATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Verb synonyms: to raise something higher, hoist it up.

clue.text: One Parisian in mime breaking free

indicators.note: in places the French word inside the rearranged letters
breaking signals that the word mime is broken up and its letters rearranged

parts.note: un is French for one

explanation.surface: A Parisian mime artist breaks free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' rearranges MIME to IMME, and 'in' places UN inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Exempt, as in free from a duty or protected from a disease.

clue.text: Teeth that you floss look spotless, finally

indicators.note: finally asks for the last letter of each of the words before it

explanation.surface: Dental advice: teeth you floss come out gleaming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' takes the last letters of five words.
explanation.definitionFit: Elephants' and walruses' long protruding teeth are of this kind.

clue.text: Zero tax: a tiny bit charged: applause follows

parts.note: the figure 0 looks like the letter O
VAT is value added tax, a sales tax in Britain
an ion is an electrically charged atom or particle

explanation.surface: A tax cut announced, with a tiny levy, is greeted by cheers.
explanation.walkthrough: VAT is Britain's sales tax. 'charged' looks like taxed but means electrically charged.
explanation.definitionFit: Sustained enthusiastic clapping from an audience, often standing.

clue.text: Theatre operator needing new common currency to press forward

parts.note: the euro is the single currency shared by many European nations
to surge on is to push ahead

explanation.surface: A theatre manager needing new euros to push ahead with plans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Theatre' is the operating theatre, not a playhouse.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist who operates on the brain does so in an operating theatre.

clue.text: Flier showing what Madame Tussauds must pay?

definitions.meaning: a bird, specifically a small African finch with a red beak
Madame Tussauds is a London museum of wax figures, so it pays a bill for wax

explanation.surface: A leaflet revealing the wax museum's expenses.
explanation.walkthrough: Madame Tussauds is London's waxwork museum; 'Flier' looks like a leaflet but is a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A small finch named for its sealing-wax-red beak; punningly, an invoice for candle material.

clue.text: Morbid person, we hear, remains in stew

indicators.note: we hear signals that the word is taken by its sound, not spelling

parts.note: a ghoul is someone with an unhealthy interest in death
ash is what remains after burning

explanation.surface: A grim character's remains end up in a stew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' turns GHOUL into its sound-alike GOUL; 'remains' looks like a verb but is ASH.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hungarian dish of meat and vegetables seasoned with paprika, a kind of stew.

clue.text: Weight condition's range

parts.note: mass is a measure of weight
if introduces a condition; the 's is a link meaning has

explanation.surface: A weight condition places something within a range.
explanation.definitionFit: A compact mountain mass or group of peaks forms a range.

clue.text: Use Cockney's microwave?

indicators.note: a Cockney, a working-class Londoner, drops the H at the start of words

parts.note: to microwave food is to heat it, warm it through

explanation.surface: A Londoner's way of telling you to use the microwave.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys (East Londoners) traditionally drop initial H.
explanation.definitionFit: To consume completely, as resources are used up or food is devoured.

clue.text: Penurious husband at last raised flag

indicators.note: raised in a down clue means the letters are read upwards, backwards

parts.note: penurious means very poor

indicators.note: at last takes the final letter of husband

explanation.surface: A poor husband finally hoists a flag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' reverses POORD in this down entry; 'flag' looks like a banner but is a verb meaning wilt.
explanation.definitionFit: To flag is to tire and sag, to wilt or hang down limply.
